name: Match Creek Motors
summary: Match Creek Motors rebuilds a broken car one priced task at a time, funded by wrenches earned from a match-three puzzle running alongside it. A returning cast, led by the player's best friend Aaron and the shop's accountant Brooke, narrates the first project step by step, and the finished car is sold through a sequential, blind negotiation with three buyers rather than a simple reveal. A second balance, gold coins, grows throughout the same play and is sold directly in the shop, with nothing shown that it buys.
teaser: Match Creek Motors ends its first car with a blind negotiation: three buyers, one offer at a time, no way to see what's still coming.

observations.name: App Store listing
observations.observed: The App Store lists Match Creek Motors under a subtitle read as Solve Puzzles, modify rides, with screenshots of car customization and the match-three board, a video preview, and a description covering the opening story and features. The listing shows an in-app event card described as a new obstacle, a toy car, happening now. The rating shown is 4.8 out of 5 from about 24,000 ratings, in the puzzle, car customization and vehicle game simulation categories, rated 13+, from developer Hutch Games Limited, available in English and 11 or more other languages at 1.23 GB, for iPhone and iPad. The last update shown was two weeks before this analysis, with updates roughly once or twice a month before that.

observations.name: Reviews on the listing
observations.observed: The listing surfaces a mix of reviews, with Most helpful including one titled Can't complain, one Really good game and one Avoid this game. Favorable reviews praise the graphics, the builds, the choice of parts and the short time needed to finish a vehicle. Critical reviews describe the game as mostly match-three with little car customization and no driving, one reporting being stuck around level 50 even with all boosters and wishing for a pay-to-skip option, and one criticizing the headlight options on a specific car model. These are App Store statements rather than behavior shown in this analysis.

observations.name: Tracking permission first
observations.observed: On first launch, the first thing Match Creek Motors shows is the system request asking whether the app may track the user across other companies' apps and websites, with no screen before it explaining why. A loading screen showing a car and a barn follows.

observations.name: Terms confirmation
observations.observed: The next screen reads a request to confirm having read and agreed to the terms of service and privacy and cookie policies, with a Confirm button beneath it and no decline path described.

observations.name: The opening letter
observations.observed: The game opens on a letter addressed to Max, the player's character, from his brother Mitch, asking Max to come manage the family garage in Match Creek while Mitch deals with trouble that requires him to leave town. A photo of three other characters, Aaron, Brooke and Mitch, appears with the letter. The player's character isn't shown in the photo and isn't introduced beyond the name Max.

observations.name: Optional account save
observations.observed: A button showing a rotating cloud sits in the top left corner from the opening letter onward. Tapping it opens a Save Progress screen inviting sign-in with Apple as the only option. Match Creek Motors never separately prompts the player to create an account; account creation is optional and reachable from this button or from Settings at any time.

observations.name: Story introduction
observations.observed: A dialogue sequence introduces the garage's cast: Aaron, the player's best friend, first appears stern before smiling and giving a bear hug with haptic feedback; Brooke, the accountant and the player's high school sweetheart, tells the pair to restore the 1970 GMC Jimmy so it can be sold, since Mitch left them without help and clients are waiting. A Skip button sits at the top of the dialogue throughout. The exchange sets both a business goal, restoring and selling the truck, and an unresolved personal thread between Aaron's comment and the player's history with Brooke.

observations.name: First car arrives
observations.observed: Aaron asks for help getting the GMC Jimmy into the workshop, and the car rolls into the garage in a 3D scene. The first project's car is fixed by the story; no choice of car is offered at this point.

observations.name: First home screen
observations.observed: On the first home screen, Aaron's face appears with a prompt to head to the task list, which is enlarged, ringed and glowing with an arrow pointing at it while everything else is dimmed. The home screen also shows a hearts counter shown full, a gold coin balance read as one thousand, a second balance the player has 300 of, a photo button, a settings button and a match-three play button in the bottom right.

observations.name: The strip-down task
observations.observed: The task list shows a track running from a broken car to a fully finished one, with two boxes placed between them along the way. Aaron says tasks cost points and asks for the first one, Strip Down, priced at 150 wrenches. Tapping it deducts the wrenches, lifts the car, removes its parts, and leaves a clean shell, after which Aaron says it's time to add some parts and new tasks appear starting with the front of the car.

tags.confidence: directly observed, the wrench balance is seen rising from match-3 wins and falling by each task's stated cost
confidences: directly observed, the wrench balance is seen rising from match-3 wins and falling by each task's stated cost
tags.rationale: Wrenches meet every required condition: a quantified balance (O9, O34), a repeatable non-paid acquisition path through winning levels (O14, O16), stored units that carry between activities, deliberately selected exchanges for car tasks at stated prices (O11, O17), and a balance reduction on each exchange (O10). The app's own explainer ties the units to winning levels (O34). No paid path for wrenches is observed, so Hard Currency does not apply to this balance.
tags.alternativeConsidered: Experience Points, rejected because wrenches are spent and reduced rather than accumulated toward a threshold. Energy, rejected because the user chooses which task to buy rather than having units consumed by participating.

observations.name: Guided task selection
observations.observed: With the screen still dimmed, Aaron points at the task list again. The available tasks are front fenders at 150, headlights at 100, front bumper at 120 and hood at 200, with 150 wrenches remaining; only front fenders is highlighted and selectable, though headlights and the front bumper are also affordable at that balance. The hood is unaffordable at 200.

observations.name: First style choice
observations.observed: Aaron asks the player to choose the option that shows off their style, and the player picks one of three fender options; tapping an option shows it on the car with a short bounce. Aaron closes the step approvingly. The three options are described only as keeping it classic or giving it a twist, with no text describing how they differ or what result each produces.

observations.name: Pointer to the puzzle
observations.observed: With the screen still dimmed, Aaron moves from the task list to the play button, saying more points are needed. The level 1 screen sets a target of 12 turbos and offers a row of breakers to select from, all shown locked.

tags.name: Challenge

observations.name: End of guidance
observations.observed: When the home screen returns after the first match-three win, nothing is dimmed and no pointer or character leads the player; the only cue is an exclamation mark on the task list. This is the first point at which the player acts without being led. Onboarding asks no questions, shows no progress indicator, and collects no preferences; the story choices don't branch the flow, and the sequence is the same regardless.

observations.name: The earn-and-spend loop
observations.observed: Match Creek Motors repeats one unit throughout the first project: win a match-three level, receive wrenches and gold coins, spend the wrenches on a car task, and return to a level once the balance runs short. The balance was spent to zero several times across the project. Eleven match-three levels were played to complete the first car in this analysis.

observations.name: Task list rules
observations.observed: Car work is organized as a list of tasks, each carrying its own wrench cost, and completing a task can bring several new ones onto the list at once. After the guided opening, the player chooses which available task to take next. The final task on the list is selling the finished car. Stated costs seen include 150 wrenches for stripping the car down, 150 for the front fenders, 100 for headlights, 120 for the front bumper and 200 for the hood. A task can sit on the list priced above the current balance until more wrenches are earned.

observations.name: Match-three level rules
observations.observed: Each match-three level states a collection target at the top of the board, a single shape on the earliest levels and combined shapes with breakable crates on later ones. Levels took 15 to 20 seconds each in this analysis and were described as easy early on, growing harder as they progressed. Level 9 was reached by the side-mirror task, and level 11 by the end of the project.

observations.name: The buyer negotiation
observations.observed: When the car is finished, a scout named Logan is introduced, and the accountant Brooke opens the final task: negotiating a sale. Three buyers make offers one at a time, shown as cards the player drags left to reject or right to accept, without seeing the offers still to come. The first offer, 20 gold coins and one booster, is called a lowball by Brooke, who tells the player to reject it; a second offer of 20 gold coins follows; a third, three boosters and 100 gold coins, is the one Brooke says to accept. Accepting triggers a celebration animation. Brooke's instructions determined which card was rejected and which was accepted in this first sale.

systemView: This is a medium system. Wrenches are the currency every restoration task draws from, earned only by winning a match-three level, so the puzzle and the car are locked together for the length of the project. A second balance, gold coins, and a running heart count both grow or sit alongside that same loop without a shown rule tying them back into it, and the project closes with a negotiated sale rather than an automatic reward.

mechanicWriteups.name: Cosmetic Customization
mechanicWriteups.summary: Each restoration task offers three unlabeled style options for a part, applied on tap and revisable later in a dedicated garage view.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Match Creek Motors opens most restoration tasks on a choice among three presentations of the same part, framed as showing off the player's own style. Some tasks are settings rather than physical parts, such as a suspension-height slider offering low rider, high rider or normal. A separate garage view lists every change made to the car and lets the player revisit and change an earlier choice.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Tapping an option applies it to the 3D car immediately, with a short bounce animation, before the choice is confirmed. No option carries a description, a stated effect or a price difference from the other two.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Match Creek Motors frames every choice as a matter of look rather than function, and nothing in the app ties a specific choice to the offers the finished car later receives; whether a build's parts affect the sale isn't something this write-up can describe.
findings: Most restoration tasks offer three style options for a part, applied on tap.
Some tasks are settings, such as ride height, rather than physical parts.
A garage view lists every change made and lets the player revise an earlier choice.
Match Creek Motors doesn't state a price or outcome difference between a task's three options.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: a part task's three-option choice screen; the garage view listing installed changes.

mechanicWriteups.name: Challenge
mechanicWriteups.summary: Each match-three level states a piece-collection target that grows more complex over successive levels, and every level played ends in a win.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Match Creek Motors states a collection target at the top of the board for each level, starting with a single shape and later combining several shapes with crates that must be broken. The remaining count updates as pieces are matched, and a completion screen follows a cleared target.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The target sits at the top of the board throughout a level, and the completion screen appears immediately once it's cleared, paying wrenches and gold coins.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Match Creek Motors doesn't show a move limit, a timer or what happens when a level isn't cleared; every level played in this analysis reached its target.
findings: Each level states a piece-collection target at the top of the board.
Later levels combine several shapes and add crates that must be broken.
A completion screen pays wrenches and gold coins once the target is cleared.
Match Creek Motors doesn't show a move limit, a timer or an unsuccessful outcome.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: a level's target display at the top of the board; the completion screen paying wrenches and gold coins.

mechanicWriteups.name: Boosters

mechanicWriteups.presented: The selection row sits on the pre-level screen, with a choice of whether to start the level carrying them or not.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Match Creek Motors doesn't say what one of these items does inside a level, or whether the count of three falls after it's used; this write-up describes the selection screen and the grants, not an effect that wasn't shown.
findings: From level 9, a pre-level screen offers three of an item the player can start the level with.
The same items, or similarly named ones, are granted through the sale and at project completion.
Match Creek Motors doesn't state what one of these items does during a level.

mechanicWriteups.noting: The count stayed full throughout this analysis, and Match Creek Motors doesn't show a heart leaving the counter at any point; what actually removes one isn't something this write-up can describe.

mechanicWriteups.name: Soft Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: Wrenches earned from winning match-three levels are spent entirely on the restoration tasks that rebuild the current car.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Match Creek Motors pays wrenches for winning a match-three level, and wrenches are spent on the individual tasks that make up a car's restoration, each stated at its own price. When the wrench balance can't cover the next task, the player returns to a level to earn more.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The wrench balance sits on the home screen throughout play, and an explainer reached by tapping it states plainly that winning levels is how points are earned. Every task states its wrench cost before it's chosen.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Match Creek Motors ties the wrench balance to exactly one use, buying the next task, with winning a level as the only way stated to refill it.
findings: Wrenches are earned by winning match-three levels and spent on restoration tasks.
An in-app explainer states that winning levels is how wrenches are earned.
Each task states its wrench cost before it's chosen.
No other source of wrenches, and no other use for them, appears anywhere else.

mechanicWriteups.name: Hard Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: Gold coins grow throughout the same loop that earns wrenches and are also sold directly in four packs, with no purchase shown for anything they buy.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Match Creek Motors sells gold coins in four packs in the shop. The same balance also grows from winning match-three levels, from the reward boxes on the project track, from the sale, and from completing the project.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The gold coin balance sits on the home screen beside the wrench balance, and tapping it opens the shop directly. The four packs are listed together with their prices.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Match Creek Motors shows every route into the gold coin balance, earned and bought, but no route out; nothing in this write-up claims a price or use for gold coins beyond what's shown, because nothing spending them appears anywhere in the app.

mechanicWriteups.summary: Two named leaderboards, reached through Apple's Game Center, rank players in separate Friends and Global scopes.

sectionLeadIns.onboarding: Match Creek Motors runs a fully guided first project before handing control to the player. This section covers the App Store listing, first launch, and the guided steps that introduce spending and choices.
sectionLeadIns.core-loop: Winning a match-three level is what funds every step of a car's restoration. This section covers the loop between the two, the task list and its choices, and the negotiation that closes the project.
sectionLeadIns.goals: Match Creek Motors tracks the current car's progress and the wider set of projects ahead at once. This section covers the project track's reward boxes, project completion, the story scene that follows it, the missions map, and the achievement list.
sectionLeadIns.access: Match Creek Motors locks a player profile and a pre-level item selection behind conditions it states only partly. This section covers both.
sectionLeadIns.economy: Match Creek Motors runs two currencies and a counted item alongside its match-three levels. This section covers wrenches, gold coins and the pre-level breakers.
sectionLeadIns.social: Match Creek Motors' only comparison surfaces are two leaderboards reached through Apple's Game Center.

sectionCards.onboarding: Fifteen observations carry the player from the App Store listing through a fully guided first project, with the garage's cast directing each step before handing over control.
sectionCards.core-loop: Winning a match-three level pays wrenches that fund the next restoration task, a loop that repeats through customization choices, crew comments and a blind sale negotiation.
sectionCards.goals: Reward boxes on the project track, the project's own completion, a missions map of cars still ahead, and an achievement list all track progress at once.
sectionCards.access: A player profile and the pre-level breaker selection each stay locked behind conditions Match Creek Motors doesn't fully explain.
sectionCards.economy: Wrenches fund the current car alone, gold coins are sold and earned with no shown use, and hearts and boosters each sit without a shown consumption rule.
sectionCards.social: Two named leaderboards rank players by win streak and first-try wins, reached entirely through Apple's Game Center.

sectionCards.monetization: A coin shop sells four gold coin packs, the only purchase surface reached in this analysis.

proposedTags.name: Serialized Story Reveal
proposedTags.draftDefinition: A serialized story reveal is a narrative scene that the product releases when the user completes a defined unit of progression, which advances a continuing story and ends on at least one question the product states as unresolved and carries forward to later units.
proposedTags.conditions: A progression built from discrete units, such as projects, chapters or episodes; a persistent cast or narrative thread spanning those units; release of the scene tied to completing a unit rather than to time; an explicit statement in the scene that a question remains open ("that's a mystery for another time").
proposedTags.whyNotCovered: Milestone covers the recognition of reaching a point on a progression and its rewarded and unlocking variants, but not the release of narrative content that advances a continuing story and carries an open question across units. Companion does not apply because the characters are not acquired, assigned or developed. No approved entry covers story content as the payoff of completing progression.
proposedTags.recurrenceElsewhere: The Chrome Valley Customs analysis (session 03 Mar 2026) records a partial second instance. Its O29 describes a continuing story across episodes: the garage was robbed by an antagonist, Greasy Joe, the first build is framed as the chance to make things right, and the second episode hints that someone is ripping off car businesses across town and that more about Greasy Joe may be found. The second episode opens only after the first car is completed and revealed (its O24), and no time-based release of story is recorded, so the story there advances on completion rather than on time. The Greasy Joe thread is carried across the episode boundary as an open question. Two differences limit the match: story beats in Chrome Valley Customs arrive with each batch of tasks (its O17) rather than in one closing scene, and the hint about Greasy Joe is recorded at the opening of the second episode rather than stated as unresolved at the close of the first. That record also covers only one completed episode, so it does not show whether the thread is resolved, extended or dropped later. The Royal Match analysis describes its king as a narrative host; it has not been checked here for this shape.
proposedTags.caveat: Only one project and its closing scene are observed. Whether the next project resolves or extends the open question about Mitch, whether scenes can be replayed, and whether story release ever depends on anything other than project completion are not observed. The introduction (O7) precedes any progression and is not itself a reveal under this definition. Two pieces of evidence would settle the proposal. First, a Match Creek Motors session that completes a second project and records whether the question about Mitch is carried into that project's scenes, extended, resolved or dropped, and whether the scene is released on completion alone. Second, a second app showing the same shape in full: a scene released on completing a unit that states a question as open and carries it into a later unit. Chrome Valley Customs comes closest, and a session there that completes a second episode and records whether the Greasy Joe thread is picked up at its close would settle whether it qualifies.

system.tagline: A match-three puzzle whose every win funds a car restoration that ends in a blind sale negotiation, with achievements and leaderboards routed entirely outside the game.
system.overview: Match Creek Motors treats its match-three levels as pure funding for a car-restoration story: every level won pays wrenches that go straight to the next priced task on the current car, each carrying a cosmetic choice the crew sometimes comments on. Gold coins, hearts and boosters all sit around the same loop without a shown rule connecting them to it, and the project closes with a sale negotiated across three sequential, blind offers rather than a straightforward reveal.
system.loop: Winning a match-three level pays wrenches and gold coins, and the numbered level count climbs by one. Wrenches fund the next restoration task, each carrying a three-option cosmetic choice, and reward boxes along the project track pay gold coins as the car nears completion. Selling the finished car through a sequential, blind negotiation closes the project, paying a final round of gold coins and boosters, and opens a story scene before the next car is chosen. A running heart count and a pre-level booster selection both sit beside the loop without a shown consumption rule, and a locked player profile reads a level-14 requirement against the same numbered level count the loop advances. Gold coins are also sold directly in the shop, the same balance the loop already grows for free.
system.keyInsight: The match-three level is the one action every other system in Match Creek Motors either feeds or reads. Wrenches, gold coins, the numbered level count, and the milestone boxes on the project track all come from winning the same levels, so the achievement and leaderboard systems are the only two pieces that don't touch that loop at all, sitting entirely outside the game in Game Center instead.
system.whatMakesItWork: Because nearly every resource traces back to the same match-three level, the restoration loop needs nothing else to keep running: wrenches fund it, gold coins accumulate alongside it, and the project track's milestones mark its progress, all from the same repeated action. The sale negotiation is the one point where the game asks for a real decision rather than leading one, though the first instance played out was still narrated by the cast rather than left open.

roles.role: Each match-three level is a bounded objective with a stated collection target, the action every currency and level-count advance in the system comes from.
Wrenches earned from every level fund the current car's restoration tasks, with no other stated use.
Each restoration task carries a three-option style choice, applied and revisable, with no stated effect on anything the game tracks.
Two reward boxes on the project track pay out as the car nears completion, separate from the project's own completion reward.
A pre-level selection screen offers three of an item from level 9 onward, with no shown effect or reduction on use.
A hearts counter, named lives by the app itself, sits beside the loop with no shown consumption rule.
A locked player profile states a level-14 requirement against the same numbered level count the loop advances.
Gold coins are sold directly in four packs and also earned throughout the loop, with no shown spend anywhere in the app.
Two named boards rank players by win streak and first-try wins, reached entirely outside the game through Game Center.
A list of collectible achievements is reached entirely through Game Center, with no achievement named or shown inside the game itself.

connections.title: Every level pays wrenches
connections.desc: Winning a match-three level pays a wrench reward every time.
connections.effect: Wrenches have exactly one source, so funding the next restoration task always means playing another level.

connections.title: Every level also pays gold coins
connections.desc: Winning a match-three level pays a gold coin reward alongside its wrenches.
connections.effect: The second balance accrues from ordinary play, not only from purchases.

connections.title: Winning advances the numbered level count the gate reads
connections.desc: The numbered match-three level climbs by one with every level won, the same count the player-profile requirement is stated against.
connections.effect: Reaching the profile's level-14 requirement, whatever it turns out to measure, runs through the same repeated action as everything else.

connections.title: Wrenches buy the tasks that carry each style choice
connections.desc: Every restoration task, each opening a three-option style choice, is bought with wrenches.
connections.effect: The currency spent on cosmetic choices is earned from the same puzzle that funds the rest of the project.

connections.title: Task spending advances the car toward the track's reward boxes
connections.desc: Completing coin-priced tasks moves the project track forward, past the two reward boxes placed along it.
connections.effect: Spending wrenches on the car is also what triggers the track's own milestone payouts.

connections.title: Project completion pays a final round of gold coins
connections.desc: The Episode complete screen grants gold coins alongside boosters once the project is finished.
connections.effect: Finishing a car adds directly to the same balance the shop also sells.

connections.title: Project completion grants boosters alongside coins
connections.desc: The project-completion reward grants a number of boosters together with its coin payout.
connections.effect: Finishing a car restocks whatever boosters are, independent of the pre-level breaker selection.

connections.title: Both systems are reached through the same Game Center surface
connections.desc: Achievements and leaderboards both route through Settings, Account, and Apple's Game Center, invisible during normal play.
connections.effect: Neither system is discoverable from inside the game itself; both depend on the player looking in Settings.
